## #120 — Configurable CSDM service mapping for instance CIs

Relate instance CIs up to a Service so change **Impacted Services** rolls up — but never impose it. CSDM is the customer's domain, so mapping is opt-in with a safe default.

### What ships
- Admin-only config table `x_askew_ifr_cmdb_config` with `service_mode`:
  - **none** (DEFAULT) — leave the customer's services untouched
  - **link** — relate every instance to a chosen existing `cmdb_ci_service`
  - **create** — auto-create/maintain an Application Service per instance
- Relationship `Depends on::Used by` (service depends on instance) → an instance/software change impacts the service.
- Pure `planServiceMapping` unit tested (10 cmdb-plan tests, 143 total).

### CMDB lifecycle fix (also repairs #118)
A scoped app cannot DELETE global CMDB records (`deleteRecord` returns false) — so the #118 software prune and the #120 reconcile were non-functional. Both now **retire** via `operational_status` (updates cross-scope; retired CIs are excluded from change impact — the CSDM-correct lifecycle). Present CIs → Operational, absent → Retired.

### Verified live (dev392349)
- `create` → "AU Dev Service" made, related Depends on::Used by AU Dev; AU Dev CI now shows 5 software + 1 service.
- Reconcile: mode `none` → service **Retired**; mode `create` → **Operational**.
- 143 tests green · build clean · store gate pass (manifest bumped to 20 tables, admin ACLs on config).

### Council
- **mmax** — flagged name-not-refreshed, no mode-change reconcile, rel-type dup; on-instance diagnosis found the cross-scope delete block. All fixed via retire-based reconcile + name upsert. Documented minor limit: a changed `relationship_type` may leave the prior relationship (cross-scope rel delete not permitted).

Azure Monitor to ServiceNow: three settings we need confirmed before build

We are wiring Azure Monitor alerts into ServiceNow so they raise, update and auto close incidents through the MID Server. Before we build, we need the Azure side to commit to three settings on the action group. Everything downstream depends on them, so we pin them first.

1. Send the Common Alert Schema

Enable the common alert schema on the action group action, so every alert arrives with schemaId of azureMonitorCommonAlertSchema. In the portal this is the Yes toggle on the action, or set useCommonAlertSchema to true through the Action Groups REST API. Our normaliser reads a fixed set of fields from data.essentials. With one standard envelope we map once. Without it, each alert type has its own shape and we hand map every one, which is slower to build and more fragile to run.

2. Send both Fired and Resolved

Azure must send the Resolved transition, not only the Fired one. Each alert carries monitorCondition, which is Fired when the alert fires and Resolved when the underlying condition clears. The Resolved message is what auto closes the ticket in ServiceNow, and we key the close on monitorCondition. If Azure sends Fired only, every incident stays open until a person closes it by hand. This is the single most important item on the list.

One caveat from the Microsoft schema: the resolvedDateTime timestamp is currently populated for metric alerts only. That is fine for us, because we drive the close from monitorCondition rather than from resolvedDateTime.

3. Carry a stable dedup key across Fired and Resolved

The same logical alert must carry a stable identifier on both its Fired and Resolved messages. We use originAlertId when present, otherwise alertRule combined with the affected resource id taken from alertTargetIDs. This key does two jobs: it stops a flapping alert from storming hundreds of duplicate tickets, and it is how a close finds and resolves the matching open incident rather than opening a second one.

One more, if we bind incidents to configuration items

If we want each incident linked to the affected CI in the CMDB, we rely on the resource identity in the essentials section. Microsoft documents configurationItems as the field ITSM systems use to correlate alerts to resources in a configuration management database, and alertTargetIDs carries the Azure Resource Manager ids of the affected targets. Please confirm whether CI binding is in scope, and that these fields are populated.

Context

We understand the feed is alerts only, with no event control at our end. That is workable, but it puts all the weight on these settings being right at source. Please confirm each can be enabled, or flag any that cannot, so we can plan around it.

Reference field list from data.essentials, for the Azure team: monitorCondition, originAlertId, alertId, alertRule, alertRuleId, alertTargetIDs, configurationItems, targetResourceType, targetResourceGroup, severity, signalType, description, firedDateTime, resolvedDateTime.

  • Create and manage action groups in Azure Monitor - configuring the webhook action.
  • Samples of Azure Monitor alert payloads - the Fired and Resolved payload shape, including data.essentials.

Event Management licensing: what we need to confirm before we pick the build path

The whole solution forks on one question: is ServiceNow Event Management licensed on the target instance? This decides how alerts are de-duplicated and how incidents are opened and closed, and it changes how much we build by hand. We should resolve it early, because nothing past the shared core moves until we know the answer.

Why it matters

  • Path A, Event Management licensed. Alerts land as native events, de-duplicate and form alerts in the platform, and an alert rule opens the incident. This is mostly configuration, close to out of the box.
  • Path B, no Event Management. We build a custom intake: a staging table, a scripted web service, and hand written de-duplication and idempotency. It works, but it is extra build now and extra maintenance forever. The Event Management subscription cost is what you weigh against that custom effort.

What we need to find out

  1. Is Event Management subscribed? Event Management is a separate paid subscription. It is not active by default and can only be turned on by ServiceNow personnel. Confirm entitlement with the customer ServiceNow account manager or procurement.
  2. Is it already active on the target instance? Check whether the Event Management plugin, com.glideapp.itom.snac, is active, whether the event and alert tables are present, and whether the evt_mgmt roles exist. Active means Path A is ready to build.
  3. Which instances are covered? Activation normally covers production and sub production together. Confirm both, so we can build and test on sub production before production.
  4. If not licensed, is there appetite to license it? If the answer is no and will stay no, we commit to Path B and price the extra custom build.

How to confirm quickly

The fastest confirmation is the customer ServiceNow account manager, who can state the entitlement and arrange activation, usually within a few days. In parallel, an administrator can check the plugin and roles on the instance to read the current state.

Reference documents

The fork and its decision gate are recorded in our design set:

  • adr/0001-pivot-ready-alert-ticketing.md - the design decision, the two paths, and the gate.
  • architecture.md - the layers and the data path for each path.

Grounding: that Event Management is a separate subscription activated by ServiceNow personnel, the plugin id, and the account manager activation path are from the ServiceNow product documentation, Australia release.

Follow-up: metrics worth adding to your rerank/embed testing

Hi Davey,

Quick add-on to the last note. My earlier benches leaned on recall@k, which is binary at each cutoff. If you widen the scorecard with a few more metrics, your results will tell you a lot more per run. Here is what I would add and why, ranked.

Rank-aware (how well ordered, not just present)

  • MRR (mean reciprocal rank). Captures how far down the correct chunk lands, not just whether it made top-1. If a model demotes the right answer from rank 1 to rank 4, recall@1 sees a flat miss but MRR sees the distance. The cleanest single number for ranking quality.
  • nDCG@10. The IR standard, position-weighted and able to handle graded or multi-relevant results. Rewards keeping the right chunk high. This is the number most papers and vendors quote, so it makes your results comparable.

Noise and cost (what recall@k ignores)

  • Precision@k. Of the top-K you feed the composer, how much is actually relevant. Recall@k says the answer is somewhere in the set; precision@k says how much noise rode along, which drives composer accuracy and token spend.

The metric that actually matters

  • End-to-end answer correctness and faithfulness. Retrieval recall is a proxy for "can the composer answer." Add a small answer-level check: is the composed answer correct, and is it grounded in the retrieved chunks. A pipeline can win on retrieval and still hallucinate, so this is the real gate.

Slicing and rigour (cheap, high leverage)

  • Break every metric down by content type (chunk_kind and domain). Reporting each metric sliced by paragraph vs table vs list vs schema-object is the highest-value add. It reuses your existing runs and shows whether a model behaves differently on prose vs reference content, which is exactly the kind of split that changes an architecture decision.
  • Bootstrap 95% confidence intervals. On corpora of a few hundred to a couple of thousand queries, a 2 to 3 point gap can be noise. A CI or a paired bootstrap keeps you from over-reading a coin toss.
  • Answerable rate (retrievability ceiling). The fraction of queries where any relevant chunk exists in the corpus at all. It separates a retriever miss from a corpus gap, and sets the ceiling every other metric is chasing.

If you only add three

MRR, nDCG@10, and the per-chunk_kind breakdown. Together they turn a flat "model A beat model B" into "model A wins on prose by X, loses on reference by Y, at these ranks", which is the version you can actually act on.

Cheers,
Daniel

Reranker testing on the RAG, and what it means for the Qwen embed/rerank plan

Hi Davey,

Before you sink L40S time into Qwen3-8B rerank and embed, here is what I already found the hard way on the docs-rag stack (ServiceNow/vendor PDF retrieval). Short version: the reranker stage lost, and the reason it lost is specific to our content, so it is worth knowing before you test.

Headline finding: cross-encoder rerankers invert on ServiceNow content

On real ServiceNow material, adding a cross-encoder reranker pushed the correct chunk out of top-1 (recall@1 dropped 15 to 30 points) while keeping recall@10 high. The cause is structural: cross-encoders are trained on natural-language question/answer pairs, so they read list, reference and CMDB-schema chunks (think cmdb_ci_appl_sap_scs, Display name = ...) as "not answer-like" and demote them.

This was not a one-model fluke. Two independent rerankers failed the same way: bge-reranker-v2-m3 (local, via TEI) and Cohere rerank-v3.5 (top-tier commercial). Two unrelated rerankers inverting identically is what made the call solid.

What won instead: hybrid retrieval, no reranker

Dense (embeddinggemma-300m) plus BM25 over a Postgres tsvector, fused with Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF, k=60), top-K straight to the composer. BM25 is built for the snake_case identifier matches that dominate our corpus, and adding it to dense lifted recall@1 by about 21 points. No reranker beat that on reference-shaped content.

The numbers (recall@1 is the metric that matters here)

BenchCorpusdensehybrid (d+BM25+RRF)dense+rerankreranker
v7396 CMDB0.57—0.42bge-v2-m3
v8396 CMDB0.480.690.39Cohere v3.5
v9273 api-ref0.340.460.40Cohere v3.5
v9b1924, 4 domains0.290.520.37Cohere v3.5

Embedder selection (earlier bench): embeddinggemma-300m won at recall@1 0.96, beating arctic-embed2, bge-m3, nomic v1.5 and v2-moe, mxbai, granite, and qwen3-embedding-4B. BM25 on its own reached recall@1 up to 0.47 because it loves the identifiers.

What this means for your Qwen3-8B test

  • Embedding is the test worth running. Qwen3-Embedding-8B as a dense embedder is a fair, open A/B against embeddinggemma-300m. The 300m model won at small size, but an 8B might lift dense recall@1. Genuinely unknown, worth measuring.
  • Blanket rerank is likely a dead end. Qwen3-Reranker-4B was on my list but never benched, and it is the same paradigm that inverted twice on our content. Testing it blind will most likely reproduce the bge/Cohere failure.
  • The one rerank question still open is conditional rerank by chunk type: on prose and api-reference chunks, rerank actually helped recall@5/@10 by about 5 to 6 points, even while it hurt top-1 on reference material. So the real experiment is "rerank paragraphs and sections only, bypass tables, lists, code and schema objects." If you want to test Qwen rerank, scope it to that, not the whole corpus.

Deployment gotchas that cost me time

  • Ollama has no cross-encoder rerank API. Community GGUF rerankers get silently treated as embedders, so you get garbage without an error.
  • The TEI CPU image (ONNX) fails on bge-reranker-v2-m3 (safetensors only). Use the CUDA image (Candle), which reads safetensors directly.
  • BM25 recall@1 sat at 0.01 until the tokenizer preserved snake_case. Use [a-z0-9][a-z0-9_]*, not a naive split that leaves trailing commas attached to identifiers.
  • embeddinggemma is licence-gated, so it needs an HF token set.

Suggested plan while the L40S is offline for cooling

  1. Run the Qwen3-Embedding-8B vs embeddinggemma-300m A/B first. A hosted Qwen embedding endpoint gives you the quality read in minutes without waiting for hardware.
  2. Only test Qwen rerank if you scope it to prose chunks, as the conditional experiment above.
  3. Bring the 8B work onto the L40S once cooling is sorted, since it is the only box that fits both 8B models comfortably.

Happy to walk through any of the bench harness if useful.

Cheers,
Daniel
